narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 59% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Your rejection was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. The strongest influence came from your third-year grades. You placed in the bottom decile (decile 3 = 1) among your classmates, far below the average of roughly 5.8 for students who were accepted. This low ranking strongly pushed the model toward predicting failure.

Your undergraduate GPA of 3.60 worked in your favor. It is noticeably higher than the 3.23 average of accepted students and therefore pulled the prediction toward passing. However, this positive effect was not large enough to overcome the other signals.

Your LSAT score of 26 was the third most important factor. This is substantially below the 37-point average of accepted applicants and pushed the prediction back toward failure.

Taken together, the model saw your weak class ranking in year three and low LSAT score as outweighing your solid college GPA, leading it to conclude you were more likely than not to struggle with the bar exam.

What you should do next is straightforward: focus on improving your class rank this year, retake the LSAT and aim for a much higher score, then reapply. These two changes would directly address the factors that blocked your application this time. (218 words)
